title: Quick Sort
intuition: Pick a pivot, partition smaller elements to the left and larger to the right, and recurse.
whyExists: The fastest general-purpose comparison sort in practice due to exceptional cache locality and $O(\log n)$ in-place call stack overhead.
analogy: Organizing students by height: pick one student as the reference, send all shorter students left, all taller students right, then repeat within each group.
coreIdea: The partition() subroutine picks a pivot (e.g. a[high]) and reorganizes the range so elements $< \text{pivot}$ are grouped at the start. The pivot is placed at index i + 1, which becomes its permanent sorted location, and recursive calls sort the subranges.

time.worst: O(n²) already sorted with naive pivot

complexity.reason: In-place partitioning with high CPU cache hit rates; degenerate splits trigger quadratic time.

pitfalls: Naive pivot choice on sorted arrays degrades performance to O(n²).
Quick Sort is NOT stable because swapping over long spans disrupts relative ordering.
Stack overflow on massive arrays if tail-call optimization isn't applied to the smaller partition.
